editorial:
A middle-class family in Taipei moves through ordinary days that slowly turn into big questions about life, love, and regret. NJ, the tired father, juggles a failing business deal, a brother who owes him money, and a wife who is falling apart after her mother slips into a coma. His teenage daughter Ting-Ting wrestles with guilt and first love, while his young son Yang-Yang quietly observes the world with a camera. The movie feels like a warm, honest look at how families hold together when everything feels uncertain. It moves at a gentle pace and lets small moments breathe, so you feel like you are living alongside these people rather than just watching them.

The acting is natural and deeply felt, especially from the kids, and the storytelling trusts you to notice details on your own. The downside is the long runtime and slow rhythm, which may test viewers who want fast action or clear plot twists. If you enjoy thoughtful family dramas that reward patience, this is a must.
endingExplained: In the final scenes, NJ travels to Japan for a business meeting and runs into Sherry, the woman he left years ago. They spend time together but realize they cannot go back to who they were, and NJ returns home accepting his life. At the grandmother's funeral, young Yang-Yang gives a speech saying people only see half of the truth, and he wants to show them the other half using his camera. The film closes on this quiet, hopeful note about seeing life fully.
targetAudience: Ideal for anyone who loves patient, character-driven family stories.
